report.tagline: The writing assistant that checks and improves your writing in every app, now part of an AI productivity suite under the parent company Superhuman.
report.simpleSummary: Grammarly fixes your writing as you type. It works in email, Word, Google Docs, LinkedIn and almost any website, underlining mistakes and suggesting clearer words. It was an AI product years before ChatGPT. When ChatGPT made writing help free, Grammarly had to change, so it bought the Coda docs app and the Superhuman email app, and in October 2025 renamed the whole company Superhuman, while Grammarly stays the main product.

overview.whatItDoes: Grammarly checks spelling, grammar, tone and clarity, and uses generative AI to rewrite, draft and reply. It works everywhere through a browser extension, desktop app and phone keyboard. Under the Superhuman brand, it is now bundled with Coda (docs), Superhuman Mail and Superhuman Go, an AI assistant that works across apps.
howItWorks: Install the browser extension, desktop app or mobile keyboard; it reads what you type in other apps.
Underlines show errors and suggestions; click to accept.
Generative AI can rewrite a paragraph, change tone, or draft a reply from a short prompt.
AI agents for students check citations, predict a grade and detect AI-written text.
Teams set style guides and brand tones so everyone writes the same way.
Free plan covers basic fixes; Pro unlocks full rewrites, tone and more AI prompts.
overview.valueProposition: Write clearly and confidently in any app, without copy-pasting into a separate AI tool.

businessModel.summary: Grammarly makes money from subscriptions. Individuals pay for Pro; companies pay per user for business plans. The free plan is the main way people find it. The new Superhuman suite tries to sell more per user by bundling Grammarly with Coda, Superhuman Mail and Go.

revenueStreams.detail: About $12 a month billed yearly; more if billed monthly.
Per-user pricing for teams with style guides, admin and security.
Bundles including Coda, Superhuman Mail and Go at higher prices.

businessModel.pricing: Free plan. Pro about $12 a month billed yearly (higher monthly). Enterprise: custom. Superhuman suite bundles priced separately. Prices from grammarly.com and may change; local prices in India are lower.
costDrivers: AI model costs for generative features, including fees to large language model providers
Marketing, especially paid ads and YouTube sponsorships
Engineering for apps that work across thousands of websites
businessModel.unitEconomics: A Pro user pays about $144 a year. Classic grammar checks are cheap to run, maybe a few cents a month, so old Grammarly had high margins. Generative AI rewrites cost more per use, maybe $1 to 3 a month for an active user, which cuts margins. Grammarly spends heavily on ads; if it costs $50 to $100 to win a paying user and they stay two years, it earns back that cost several times. The $1 billion from General Catalyst is to fund exactly this marketing.

howTheyGetUsers: Huge YouTube and online ad campaigns
Free plan with visible 'premium' suggestions that tease upgrades
Word of mouth among students and non-native speakers
whatBringsUsersBack: Works automatically in every app, so it is used daily
Business style guides tie teams to the product
growth.moat: Grammarly's moat is being everywhere you type, plus a habit built by tens of millions of users over a decade. Rivals like ChatGPT need you to switch windows. But Microsoft, Google and Apple are adding similar features directly into their own apps and keyboards, which weakens this moat.

northStar.metric: Weekly active users who accept at least 10 suggestions
northStar.why: Accepted suggestions mean Grammarly actually improved someone's writing. Weekly use shows the habit is alive. This north star metric tracks real help, not just installs. Guardrail metrics make sure growth does not come at the cost of trust, safety or margins.

pmLessons: Being early is not safety. A pre-ChatGPT AI product had to rethink itself when writing help became free.
Distribution inside workflows matters. Working where people type is Grammarly's real edge.
When your core is commoditised, expand the job. Grammarly bought Coda and Superhuman to become an AI work suite.
Freemium needs a clear reason to pay. Teasing premium suggestions works, but too much upsell annoys users.
Rebrands are risky. Renaming the company can confuse users of a famous product.

interviewQuestions.question: ChatGPT made writing help free. How would you keep Grammarly relevant?
interviewQuestions.hint: Name Grammarly's unique strengths: inline everywhere, habits, team style. Build on them with agents and context. Measure retention and conversion.

interviewQuestions.question: Was renaming the company Superhuman a good idea?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh brand equity of Grammarly against a broader suite story. Consider users, investors and employees. Suggest how to measure impact.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you grow paid users in India?
interviewQuestions.hint: Segment users: students, IT professionals. Price locally, add UPI, partner with colleges. Track conversion and churn.

interviewQuestions.question: Design metrics for Grammarly's AI detector.
interviewQuestions.hint: Accuracy, false positive rate, user trust, teacher adoption. Discuss harms of false accusations.

interviewQuestions.question: Microsoft adds free writing AI to Windows keyboards. What do you do?
interviewQuestions.hint: Assess overlap. Focus on cross-platform, team features and quality. Consider partnerships and pricing.
